sentences.text: Corythoraptor is named for its tall head crest, which featured a bony shell casing about 2 millimeters thick, possibly covered in keratin.

This toothless dinosaur possessed a skeleton filled with air pockets like other oviraptorids, twelve neck vertebrae with the sixth and eleventh being the longest, and it was covered in feathers with small wings.
Microanalysis of the bones shows the type specimen likely died at six or seven years old, yet three dark bands on the radius indicate it experienced seasonal growth spurts.
The animal reached about 1.6 meters in length at death, suggesting it was sexually active before reaching its maximum size with growth continuing for over eight years.
The species was first described by Chinese paleontologist Lü Junchang and colleagues in 2017.
The holotype, specimen JPM-2015-001, was found in the Late Cretaceous Nanxiong Formation near the Ganzhou Railway Station in Jiangxi, South China.
This almost complete skeleton includes the skull and lower jaw but lacks the distal tail vertebrae.
Dietary hypotheses suggest Corythoraptor was an omnivore that ate drought-resistant plants, nuts, and seeds, a view supported by stomach stones found in related species.
Although shellfish consumption has been proposed for oviraptorids, the jaw structure of Corythoraptor was not well-suited for crushing shells, and the environment likely lacked sufficient shellfish.

Researchers suggest the crest may have functioned as a resonator to detect low-frequency sounds from predators, prey, or mating calls, though it is debated whether the animal could produce these sounds as they are typically generated in the throat.
An alternative hypothesis is that the crest served for visual display of social status or fitness, though this is less supported by comparisons to modern cassowaries where casques vary little.
The Ganzhou area is renowned for high oviraptorid diversity, having yielded fossils of six other genera, suggesting these species may have partitioned food resources by targeting different sources.
The environment where Corythoraptor fossils were found was likely a lakeside setting.

Phylogenetic analyses place Corythoraptor in the family Oviraptoridae, specifically within the subfamily Citipatinae, forming a clade with Huanansaurus and closely related to Citipati, Rinchenia, and Oviraptor.
Corythoraptor lived during the late Maastrichtian stage of the Late Cretaceous, approximately 74 million years ago in the Campanian stage, in what is now Asia.
The fossil record for Corythoraptor spans the Maastrichtian stage, from 72.2 to 66 million years ago.

Cau (2024) questioned the validity of Corythoraptor, suggesting it is a junior synonym of Banji based on shared skull characteristics, while Hao and Xu (2026) proposed that Corythoraptor is a junior synonym of Huanansaurus.
